paragraphs: In the preceding review of the Constitution, I have noted most of the objections that have been raised against it and have tried to answer them. A few remain, however, that either did not fall naturally under any particular head or were forgotten in their proper places. I will take them up now. Since this subject has already been drawn out to great length, I will keep to brevity by putting all my observations on these miscellaneous points into a single paper.

The most considerable of the remaining objections is that the plan of the Convention contains no bill of rights. Among the other answers given to this, it has been pointed out on various occasions that the constitutions of several of the States are in the same position. I add that New York is one of them. Yet the opponents of the new system in this State, who profess unlimited admiration for its constitution, are among the most intemperate champions of a bill of rights. To justify their zeal, they allege two things. One is that, although the constitution of New York has no bill of rights placed at its head, it contains in the body of the document various provisions in favor of particular privileges and rights, which in substance amount to the same thing. The other is that the constitution adopts the common law and statute law of Great Britain in their full extent, and that these equally secure many other rights that it does not state.
To the first, I answer that the Constitution proposed by the Convention contains a number of such provisions, just as the constitution of this State does.

Apart from those that concern the structure of the government, we find the following. Article 1, section 3, clause 7—"Judgment in cases of impeachment shall not extend further than to removal from office, and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States; but the party convicted shall, nevertheless, be liable and subject to indictment, trial, judgment, and punishment according to law." Section 9 of the same article, clause 2—"The privilege of the writ of habeas corpus shall not be suspended, unless when in cases of rebellion or invasion the public safety may require it." Clause 3—"No bill of attainder or ex-post-facto law shall be passed." Clause 7—"No title of nobility shall be granted by the United States; and no person holding any office of profit or trust under them, shall, without the consent of the Congress, accept of any present, emolument, office, or title of any kind whatever, from any king, prince, or foreign state." Article 3, section 2, clause 3—"The trial of all crimes, except in cases of impeachment, shall be by jury; and such trial shall be held in the State where the said crimes shall have been committed; but when not committed within any State, the trial shall be at such place or places as the Congress may by law have directed." Section 3 of the same article—"Treason against the United States shall consist only in levying war against them, or in adhering to their enemies, giving them aid and comfort. No person shall be convicted of treason, unless on the testimony of two witnesses to the same overt act, or on confession in open court." And clause 3 of the same section—"The Congress shall have power to declare the punishment of treason; but no attainder of treason shall work corruption of blood, or forfeiture, except during the life of the person attainted."

It may well be asked whether, on the whole, these provisions are not as important as any in the constitution of this State. Establishing the writ of habeas corpus and prohibiting ex post facto laws and TITLES OF NOBILITY, for which our own constitution has no corresponding provision, are perhaps greater securities for liberty and republicanism than anything it contains. Creating crimes after the act was committed, which means punishing men for things that were breaches of no law when they were done, and the practice of arbitrary imprisonment have in every age been tyranny's favorite and most formidable instruments. The remarks of the judicious Blackstone(1) on the latter are well worth repeating: "To bereave a man of life, (says he) or by violence to confiscate his estate, without accusation or trial, would be so gross and notorious an act of despotism, as must at once convey the alarm of tyranny throughout the whole nation; but confinement of the person, by secretly hurrying him to jail, where his sufferings are unknown or forgotten, is a less public, a less striking, and therefore a more dangerous engine of arbitrary government." And as a remedy for this fatal evil he speaks everywhere with particular emphasis in praise of the habeas corpus act, which in one place he calls "the BULWARK of the British Constitution."(2)

I need not argue for the importance of banning titles of nobility. It may fairly be called the cornerstone of republican government, because as long as such titles are excluded, there can be no serious danger that the government will be anything but the people's own.

To the second, that is, to the pretended establishment of the common law and state law by the Constitution, I answer that they are expressly made subject "to such alterations and provisions as the legislature shall from time to time make concerning the same." They are therefore liable at any moment to repeal by the ordinary legislative power, and so have no constitutional sanction. The only purpose of the declaration was to recognize the ancient law and to remove doubts that the Revolution might have caused. It can therefore be considered no part of a declaration of rights, which under our constitutions must be meant as limitations on the power of the government itself.

It has been truly remarked several times that bills of rights were originally agreements between kings and their subjects: curtailments of prerogative in favor of privilege, reservations of rights not surrendered to the prince. Such was MAGNA CHARTA, which the barons obtained from King John with sword in hand. Such were the later confirmations of that charter by succeeding princes. Such was the Petition of Right, to which Charles I. assented at the beginning of his reign. Such also was the Declaration of Right that the Lords and Commons presented to the Prince of Orange in 1688, and which was afterward put into the form of an act of parliament called the Bill of Rights. It is evident, therefore, that in their original meaning they have no application to constitutions that are openly founded on the power of the people and carried out by their immediate representatives and servants. Here, strictly speaking, the people surrender nothing; and since they retain everything, they have no need of particular reservations. "WE, THE PEOPLE of the United States, to secure the blessings of liberty to ourselves and our posterity, do ordain and establish this Constitution for the United States of America." Here is a better recognition of popular rights than volumes of those maxims which fill the principal place in several of our State bills of rights, and which would sound much better in a treatise on ethics than in a constitution of government.

But a minute listing of particular rights is certainly far less suited to a Constitution like this one, which is intended merely to regulate the general political interests of the nation, than to a constitution that regulates every kind of personal and private concern. If the loud clamors against the plan of the Convention on this score are well founded, therefore, no word of condemnation will be too strong for the constitution of this State. But the truth is that both of them contain everything that, in relation to their objects, can reasonably be wished.

I will go further and say that bills of rights, in the sense and to the extent demanded, are not merely unnecessary in the proposed Constitution but would even be dangerous. They would list exceptions to powers that are not granted, and for that very reason would hand people a plausible excuse to claim more power than was granted. Why declare that things shall not be done when no power exists to do them? Why, for instance, say that the liberty of the press shall not be restrained, when no power is given that could impose restrictions? I do not contend that such a provision would confer a power to regulate. But it is evident that it would give men inclined to usurp power a plausible pretense for claiming it. They could argue, with some show of reason, that the Constitution should not be charged with the absurdity of guarding against the abuse of an authority that was never given, and that a provision against restraining the liberty of the press clearly implied that the national government was meant to hold a power to prescribe proper regulations for it. This is one sample of the many handles that an ill-judged zeal for bills of rights would give to the doctrine of constructive powers.

On the subject of the liberty of the press, much as has been said about it, I cannot refrain from adding a remark or two. In the first place, I observe that there is not a syllable about it in the constitution of this State. In the next place, I contend that whatever has been said about it in the constitution of any other State amounts to nothing. What does a declaration that "the liberty of the press shall be inviolably preserved" signify? What is the liberty of the press? Who can give it any definition that would not leave the utmost room for evasion? I hold this to be impracticable; and from this I infer that its security, whatever fine declarations may be inserted in any constitution respecting it, must depend altogether on public opinion and on the general spirit of the people and of the government.(3) And here, after all, as I suggested on another occasion, we must look for the only solid basis of all our rights.

One other way of looking at this matter remains, and it will conclude the point. The truth is, after all the speeches we have heard, that the Constitution is itself, in every rational sense and for every useful purpose, A BILL OF RIGHTS. The various bills of rights in Great Britain make up its Constitution, and conversely the constitution of each State is its bill of rights. And the proposed Constitution, if adopted, will be the bill of rights of the Union. Is it one object of a bill of rights to declare and specify the political privileges of the citizens in the structure and administration of the government? This is done in the most ample and precise manner in the plan of the Convention, which includes various precautions for the public security that are not to be found in any of the State constitutions. Is another object of a bill of rights to define certain immunities and modes of proceeding that relate to personal and private concerns? We have seen that this too has been attended to, in a variety of cases, in the same plan. Considering, therefore, the substantial meaning of a bill of rights, it is absurd to allege that none is to be found in the work of the Convention. It may be said that it does not go far enough, though it will not be easy to make this appear; but it cannot properly be argued that there is no such thing. It must certainly be immaterial in what order the rights of the citizens are declared, as long as they are to be found somewhere in the instrument that establishes the government. It must therefore be apparent that much of what has been said on this subject rests merely on distinctions of word and name that have nothing to do with the substance of the thing.

Another objection has been made, and from the frequency with which it is repeated it may be presumed to be relied on. It is of this kind: "It is improper (say the objectors) to confer such large powers, as are proposed, upon the national government, because the seat of that government must of necessity be too remote from many of the States to admit of a proper knowledge on the part of the constituent, of the conduct of the representative body." This argument, if it proves anything, proves that there ought to be no general government at all. For the powers that all sides seem to agree ought to be vested in the Union cannot safely be entrusted to a body that is not under every necessary control. But there are satisfactory reasons to show that the objection is in reality not well founded. Most of the arguments about distance rest on a palpable illusion of the imagination. What are the sources of information by which the people of Montgomery County must form their judgment of the conduct of their representatives in the State legislature? They can have no benefit of personal observation, which is confined to the citizens on the spot. They must therefore depend on the information of intelligent men whom they trust; and how must these men get their information? Evidently from the character of public measures, from the public newspapers, and from correspondence with their representatives and with other persons who live at the place where the legislature deliberates. This applies not to Montgomery County only but to all the counties at any considerable distance from the seat of government.

It is just as evident that the same sources of information would be open to the people about the conduct of their representatives in the general government. Whatever obstacles to quick communication distance may be supposed to create will be outweighed by the watchfulness of the State governments. The executive and legislative bodies of each State will serve as so many sentinels over the persons employed in every department of the national administration. They will be able to set up and follow a regular and effective system of intelligence. They can therefore never be at a loss to learn how the people's representatives in the national councils are behaving, and they can readily pass that knowledge on to the people. Their willingness to alert the community to anything that threatens its interests from another quarter can be relied on, if only from the rivalry of power. And we may conclude with the fullest confidence that through that channel the people will be better informed of the conduct of their national representatives than they now are, by any means they have, of the conduct of their State representatives.

It should also be remembered that the citizens who live at and near the seat of government will have the same interest as those at a distance in every question that affects the general liberty and prosperity. They will be ready to sound the alarm when necessary and to name the people behind any destructive project. The public papers will speedily carry intelligence to the most remote inhabitants of the Union.

Among the many curious objections raised against the proposed Constitution, the most extraordinary and the least plausible comes from the lack of any provision about the debts owed to the United States. This has been portrayed as a silent surrender of those debts and as a wicked scheme to protect public defaulters. The newspapers have overflowed with the most inflammatory ranting on this head. Yet nothing is clearer than that the suggestion is entirely without foundation and is the offspring of extreme ignorance or extreme dishonesty. In addition to the remarks I have made on the subject elsewhere, I shall only observe that, as it is a plain dictate of common sense, so it is also an established doctrine of political law, that "States neither lose any of their rights, nor are discharged from any of their obligations, by a change in the form of their civil government."(4)

The last objection of any consequence that I can at present recall turns on the matter of expense. Even if it were true that adopting the proposed government would cause a considerable increase of expense, this would be an objection that ought to carry no weight against the plan.

The great mass of American citizens are justly convinced that Union is the foundation of their political happiness. With few exceptions, sensible men of every party now agree that it cannot be preserved under the present system, or without radical changes. They agree that new and extensive powers ought to be granted to the national head, and that these require a different organization of the federal government, since a single body is an unsafe depositary of such ample authority. Once all this is conceded, the question of expense must be given up; for it is impossible, with any degree of safety, to narrow the foundation on which the system is to stand. The two branches of the legislature are at first to consist of only sixty-five persons, which is the same number of which Congress may be composed under the existing Confederation. It is true that this number is meant to be increased, but only to keep pace with the growth of the country's population and resources. It is evident that a smaller number would have been unsafe even at the start, and that keeping the present number at a more advanced stage of population would give the people a very inadequate representation.
Where is the dreaded increase of expense supposed to come from? One source that has been pointed to is the multiplication of offices under the new government. Let us look at this a little.

Plainly, the principal departments of administration that the present government has are the same ones the new government will need. There are now a Secretary of War, a Secretary of Foreign Affairs, a Secretary for Domestic Affairs, a Board of Treasury consisting of three persons, a Treasurer, assistants, clerks, etc. These officers are indispensable under any system and will suffice under the new one as well as the old. As for ambassadors and other ministers and agents in foreign countries, the proposed Constitution can make no other difference than to give them more respect where they reside and to make their services more useful. As for the persons to be employed in collecting the revenues, it is unquestionably true that they will make a very considerable addition to the number of federal officers; but it will not follow that this will increase public expense. In most cases it will be nothing more than an exchange of State officers for national ones. In the collection of all duties, for instance, the persons employed will belong wholly to the latter description. The States individually will need none for this purpose. What difference can it make, in point of expense, whether the officers of the customs are appointed by the State or by the United States? There is no good reason to suppose that either the number or the salaries of the latter will be greater than those of the former.

Where, then, are we to look for those additional items of expense that are supposed to swell the account to the enormous size that has been represented to us? The chief item that occurs to me concerns the support of the judges of the United States. I do not add the President, because there is now a president of Congress, whose expenses may not fall far short, if at all, of those that will be incurred for the President of the United States. The support of the judges will clearly be an extra expense, but how great it is will depend on the particular plan adopted in this matter. On no reasonable plan, however, can it amount to a sum of any material consequence.

Now let us see what will balance any extra expense that the proposed government may bring. The first thing that presents itself is that a great part of the business that now keeps Congress sitting all year will be done by the President. Even the conduct of foreign negotiations will naturally pass to him, according to general principles settled with the Senate and subject to its final approval. So it is clear that only part of the year will be needed for the sessions of the Senate and the House of Representatives. We may suppose about a fourth of the year for the House and a third, or perhaps half, for the Senate, whose extra business of treaties and appointments may account for its longer sitting. From this we may infer that, until the House of Representatives is enlarged greatly beyond its present size, there will be a considerable saving of expense from the difference between the present Congress sitting continuously and the future Congress sitting only part of the time.

But there is another circumstance of great importance from the standpoint of economy. The business of the United States has so far occupied the State legislatures as well as Congress. Congress has made requisitions, or formal requests for money, which the State legislatures have had to provide for. As a result, the sessions of the State legislatures have been prolonged far beyond what was necessary to carry out the merely local business of the States. More than half their time has frequently been spent on matters relating to the United States. Now the members who make up the legislatures of the individual States number two thousand and upward, and this body has so far performed what under the new system will be done at first by sixty-five persons, and probably at no later period by more than a fourth or fifth of that number. Under the proposed government, Congress will itself do all the business of the United States, without the intervention of the State legislatures. From then on the latter will have only the affairs of their own States to attend to, and will not have to sit for anything like as long as they have until now. This difference in the length of the State legislatures' sessions will be clear gain, and by itself will make up a saving that may be regarded as an equivalent for any additional expenses the new system may occasion.

The conclusion from these observations is that the sources of additional expense from establishing the proposed Constitution are much fewer than may have been imagined; that they are offset by considerable savings; and that, while it is doubtful on which side the scale will tip, it is certain that a less expensive government would be unequal to the purposes of the Union.
1. See Blackstone's Commentaries, Vol. 1, p. 136.
2. The same work, Vol. 4, p. 438.

3. To show that the Constitution contains a power by which the liberty of the press may be affected, people have turned to the power of taxation. It is said that duties may be laid on publications so high as to amount to a prohibition. I do not know by what logic it could be maintained that the declarations in the State constitutions in favor of freedom of the press would be a constitutional obstacle to the State legislatures' imposing duties on publications. It certainly cannot be pretended that any degree of duties, however low, would be an abridgment of the liberty of the press. We know that newspapers are taxed in Great Britain, and yet it is notorious that the press nowhere enjoys greater liberty than in that country. And if duties of any kind may be laid without violating that liberty, it is evident that the extent must depend on legislative discretion, respecting the liberty of the press, will give it no greater security than it will have without them. The same invasions of it may be carried out through taxation under the State constitutions that contain those declarations as under the proposed Constitution, which has nothing of the kind. It would be quite as meaningful to declare that government ought to be free, that taxes ought not to be excessive, etc., as that the liberty of the press ought not to be restrained.
4. See Rutherford's Institutes, Vol. 2, Book II, Chapter X, Sections XIV and XV. See also Grotius, Book II, Chapter IX, Sections VIII and IX.
